note: Five synthetic student ideas (written for this test set, not taken from anyone). The first is the idea the live walk types (apps/web/e2e/stage2-idea-literature.spec.ts, IDEA, and docs/walkthroughs/stage-2.md step 2); the other four were written to differ in what a good answer must notice: a vague topic, a school setting with minors, a sensitive topic, and a scale the student cannot reach.

idea.topic: Does a fixed bedtime routine for one week lower exam anxiety in first-year college students?
idea.resources: About sixty first-year volunteers from my own college and a short paper questionnaire.
idea.constraints: No sleep-tracking devices; the college ethics committee meets once a month.

items.good: Starts each of the five lines with the area's name and a colon (topic clarity and researchability, access to participants or data, time, resources and equipment, ethical complexity), rates it Low, Medium or High and gives one concrete sentence that could only be about this project, drawn from what the student wrote. Ends with one verdict: Proceed as planned, Proceed with these modifications (and names them) or Reconsider this topic (and says briefly why). Never says that approval is or is not required; says what to ask the supervisor or ethics committee. Here it should use the sixty volunteers, the paper questionnaire, the semester and the monthly committee in its sentences; it may rate the topic clarity High (one routine, one outcome, one group) and should note that exam weeks make recruiting hard.

idea.topic: Do students who use spaced-repetition flashcards for four weeks score higher in a Class 11 biology unit test than students who revise by re-reading?
idea.resources: Two sections of Class 11 (about 70 students) at the school where I do my teaching practicum; the class teacher has agreed.
idea.timeframe: Six weeks before the unit test
idea.constraints: I cannot change who is in which section. No budget for printed material.

items.good: Starts each of the five lines with the area's name and a colon (topic clarity and researchability, access to participants or data, time, resources and equipment, ethical complexity), rates it Low, Medium or High and gives one concrete sentence that could only be about this project, drawn from what the student wrote. Ends with one verdict: Proceed as planned, Proceed with these modifications (and names them) or Reconsider this topic (and says briefly why). Never says that approval is or is not required; says what to ask the supervisor or ethics committee. Here it should see that the two sections are fixed (not random groups), so differences between sections could be mistaken for an effect of the flashcards, and name that as a modification. It treats the students as minors: it asks what the school and the parents need to agree to, through the institution, and does not decide that for the student. Time is tight but possible.
